CHAPTER 9: THE LABOUR MARKET

THE FOUR FACTORS OF PRODUCTION (TABLE 9.1)
- Land: anything provided by nature used to produce goods/services (timber, gas, oil, water). Payment: rent.
- Labour: the physical effort used to provide goods/services (chefs, nurses, factory workers, farm labourers). Payment: wage.
- Capital: anything human-made used to produce goods/services (machinery, computers, factory premises). Payment: interest.
- Enterprise: the entrepreneur takes a risk to make a profit by bringing the other three factors together (e.g. Pat McDonagh, founder of Supermac's). Payment: profit/loss.

GOODS AND SERVICES MARKETS VS FACTOR MARKETS
- Goods and services market: individuals buy goods/services to consume them (an ice cream, a haircut); demanded in their own right.
- Factor market: firms acquire factors of production to provide goods/services (the labour market, commodity markets such as oil).
- Demand for a factor is a derived demand.
- Derived demand: demand for a factor of production not for its own sake but for its use in producing goods/services people want (timber for tables, oil for plastic).

LAND
- Economic rent: the return on any factor of production in excess of its supply price.
- Supply price of a factor: the minimum payment needed to bring the factor into use and keep it in that use.
- Bottled water example: water from a well on the firm's own land has a supply price of zero, so all earnings from it are economic rent.
- Land is unique: all its earnings are economic rent; its supply is fixed (fossil fuels are finite), so the supply curve is vertical (perfectly inelastic); it is non-specific - it has many uses (oil for fuels, plastics, chemicals, paints).

ENTERPRISE
- Entrepreneur: the person who takes a risk to make a profit by organising the other three factors.
- Enterprise is unique: it can earn a negative return (a loss); returns vary in size (losses, normal or supernormal profits); earnings are residual - paid last after all other factors.
- Entrepreneurs provide goods/services, create jobs, pay tax and boost national income and economic growth (e.g. Pat McDonagh of Supermac's, Darina Allen of Ballymaloe Cookery School).
- Role of profits: 1. encourage risk-taking; 2. a source of funds for expansion (reinvestment); 3. encourage efficiency; 4. signal how to allocate scarce resources (more coffee shops, fewer internet cafes); 5. spin-off effects - jobs created directly and indirectly (e.g. suppliers) and wide variety of goods; 6. tax on profits is government current revenue.
- How the government encourages entrepreneurship: 1. grants/advice - Enterprise Ireland helps firms start, grow, innovate and export; 31 Local Enterprise Offices (2021) for non-exporters; 2. loans - Microfinance Ireland lends up to 25,000 euro to businesses with fewer than 10 employees and turnover below 2 million euro; 3. infrastructure - the National Broadband Plan; 4. credit - the Credit Review Office helps SMEs, sole traders and farmers refused viable loans and can force a bank to lend; 5. labour market - investment in education gives a skilled workforce.

CAPITAL
- Capital: anything human-made used to produce goods and services.
- Investment: capital formation, or the production of capital goods (building a factory, buying machinery, installing computers).
- Payment is interest: money for investment is borrowed from savers through financial institutions, and the price paid by the borrower is the interest rate.
- Capital deepening: the ratio of capital to labour increases (e.g. one extra worker plus two extra machines).
- Capital widening: the ratio stays the same (e.g. one extra worker plus one extra machine).
- FDI: over 1,500 overseas firms operate in Ireland (Chapter 17).

MARGINAL EFFICIENCY OF CAPITAL (MEC)
- MEC: the extra profit from employing one extra unit of capital - extra revenue generated minus its cost.
- Example: coffee machine costs 10,000 euro, makes 7,000 cups a year at 2 euro. MEC = 14,000 - 10,000 = 4,000 euro.
- With 3,000 euro interest, cost = 13,000 euro, MEC = 1,000 euro. A higher interest rate reduces MEC - a negative (inverse) relationship. The term was first used by John Maynard Keynes in his General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money.
- Figure 9.2 (in words): interest rate on vertical axis, quantity of capital on horizontal; downward-sloping demand for capital. Point A: high interest rate, lower MEC, low investment. Point B: low interest rate, higher MEC, high investment.
- Factors determining MEC: price of the output (coffee at 3 euro: 21,000 - 10,000 = 11,000 euro); demand for the output (8,000 cups: 16,000 - 10,000 = 6,000 euro); cost of capital and interest rate (lower = higher MEC); wear and tear (breakdowns lower output and MEC).

LABOUR - BASIC TERMS
- Labour: the physical effort that goes into supplying goods/services. Payment: the wage.
- Nominal wage: the rate of pay or salary. Real wage: the purchasing power of wages.
- Example: nominal wage 20,000 euro; if inflation is 10% and pay is unchanged, the real wage falls by 10%.
- Economic rent of labour: a footballer would play for 50,000 euro (supply price) but is paid 1 million euro; economic rent = 950,000 euro.

MPP AND MRP
- Labour productivity: output produced by a worker per period of time (e.g. 20 pizzas per hour).
- Marginal physical product of labour (MPPL, also called marginal product): extra output from employing an extra unit of labour. MPPL = change in total output / change in quantity of labour.
- Marginal revenue product of labour (MRPL): extra revenue from employing an extra unit of labour. MRPL = change in TR / change in quantity of labour, or MRPL = MPPL x MR. In perfect competition MRP = MPP x Price.
- Pizza restaurant (Table 9.3, price 10 euro): workers / total output / TR / MPP / MRP:
- 1 / 10 / 100 / 10 / 100
- 2 / 25 / 250 / 15 / 150
- 3 / 42 / 420 / 17 / 170
- 4 / 50 / 500 / 8 / 80
- 5 / 56 / 560 / 6 / 60
- 6 / 60 / 600 / 4 / 40
- 7 / 62 / 620 / 2 / 20
- 8 / 63 / 630 / 1 / 10
- In theory the MRP of the last worker hired is the wage for all workers, and the downward-sloping part of the MRP curve is the demand curve for labour.
- At a wage of 170 euro the firm hires 3; at 80 euro, 4; at 60 euro, 5; at 40 euro, 6. It would not hire a 7th at 40 euro - cost 40 euro but MRP only 20 euro.
- An employer pays all workers the MRP of the last worker hired and will not pay a worker more than their MRP.

WHY THE MRP CURVE SLOPES DOWN
- Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns (LDMR): as more units of a variable factor (labour) are combined with a fixed amount of another factor (e.g. one pizza oven), the extra output eventually diminishes. Bottlenecks - chefs in each other's way, waiting for the oven ('too many cooks spoil the broth'). In the example this happened after the 3rd worker.
- Law of Demand for the firm's output: to sell extra output the firm may have to lower the price of all units, lowering MRP. E.g. 50 extra pizzas at 10 euro = 500 euro; at 8 euro = 400 euro.

FACTORS DETERMINING THE MRP OF LABOUR
- 1. Skills of workers - skilled, qualified, experienced, motivated workers are more productive; training helps.
- 2. Quality of capital - a high-spec oven raises productivity; a broken, small or slow oven lowers it.
- 3. Ability of the employer/manager to motivate staff.
- 4. Morale - working conditions, wages and incentives (e.g. target bonuses).
- 5. Selling price of the output - pizzas at 15 euro would raise MRP by 50%; at 5 euro lower it by 50%.

USEFULNESS OF MRP THEORY
- Useful when a physical product with a market price is produced.
- Limitations: service workers (retail, office, nurses, Gardai, teachers) produce no physical output, so MPP is hard to measure; public services are not sold in a market, so have no market price; hard to separate the worker's contribution from the capital's (a chef whose output doubles due to a new oven may not deserve a rise).

DEMAND FOR LABOUR
- Demand schedule (Table 9.5): wage/QL - 170/3; 80/4; 60/5; 40/6; 20/7; 10/8. Downward-sloping demand curve (DL).
- Shifts (right = more workers hired at each wage; left = fewer):
- Demand for the firm's output (derived demand) - more demand for coffee means more baristas.
- Technology - cashierless stores (Amazon Go), self-service checkouts, possible driverless taxis/buses reduce demand.
- Employers' PRSI - a rise increases the cost of employing and reduces demand.
- State subsidies - JobsPlus gives up to 10,000 euro to employers hiring from the live register; increases demand.
- FDI - low corporation tax attracts foreign firms, increasing demand.

SUPPLY OF LABOUR
- Positive relationship between wage and labour supplied: 2 euro an hour for a hotel receptionist gets no applicants, 20 euro some, 200 euro many.
- Figure 9.6 (in words): upward-sloping SL; a rise from W1 to W2 is a movement along the curve from A (Q1) to B (Q2).
- Shift right = more people willing to work at each wage; left = fewer.
- 1. Size of the working-age population - population growth, immigration, returning emigrants and less emigration shift supply right.
- 2. Labour force participation rate: the percentage of the working-age population (16-66) in the labour force (working or seeking work) = labour force / population of working age x 100. A rise shifts supply right. 2019: 56% for women, just over 68% for men (CSO).
- 3. Mobility of labour - greater mobility, greater supply.
- Occupational mobility: willingness to move from one occupation to another. Affected by qualifications/training needed (solicitor retraining as a doctor) and restrictions on numbers (limits on medicine and veterinary places).
- Geographical mobility: willingness to move location for work. Affected by age (young more willing); family situation; property prices (Galway, Cork, Dublin); availability of information (recruitment fairs, agencies); visas and work permits (EU and UK citizens unrestricted; non-EU need permits; the Critical Skills Occupations List lets employers recruit e.g. programmers, doctors from outside the EU); incentives (Dubai offers nurses and teachers free flights, accommodation, health insurance, children's education and bonuses).

LABOUR SHORTAGES
- Full employment: everyone who wants a job can find one at existing wage rates; about 4% unemployment.
- Problems: lower-quality recruits; unfilled vacancies, poorer service; higher wages to attract/retain staff, causing wage drift; cost-push inflation; Ireland less attractive for FDI.
- Wage drift: wage levels rise above negotiated levels.
- Government solutions: more visas for non-EU workers (Critical Skills Employment Permit, e.g. ICT); raise the minimum wage (up 10c to 10.20 euro in January 2021); encourage emigrants home (HSE 'Bring Them Home' 2015-2019, 1,500 euro relocation fee, 120 healthcare professionals); reduce direct taxes (Irish nurses, doctors, teachers in Dubai pay no tax - a pull factor; high Irish taxes a push factor); incentivise training in shortage areas (STEM; 'Springboard' free courses); reduce accommodation costs; provide social infrastructure (childcare, parks, playgrounds).
- Push factors encourage people to leave a place; pull factors attract them to a place.

LABOUR MARKET EQUILIBRIUM
- Equilibrium wage: the wage in a free labour market where demand for labour equals supply - no unemployment (excess supply) and no shortages (excess demand).
- Table 9.7: wage / demand / supply - 2 euro: 100,000/20,000; 4: 80,000/40,000; 6: 60,000/60,000; 8: 40,000/80,000; 10: 20,000/100,000.
- At 2 euro: excess demand of 80,000 (shortage) - upward pressure on wages. At 10 euro: excess supply of 80,000 (unemployed) - downward pressure. Equilibrium: 6 euro, 60,000 workers.
- Figure 9.9 (in words): wage on vertical axis, number of workers on horizontal; downward DemandL and upward SupplyL cross at WE = 6 euro, QE = 60,000.

THE MINIMUM WAGE
- Minimum wage: the lowest wage per hour a worker must be paid.
- February 2020: 10.10 euro for an experienced adult worker (economy growing, rising living costs and rents, to increase the incentive to work amid emerging shortages). January 2021: 10.20 euro.
- Positive implications: better standard of living for low-paid; exploitation prevented (employers paying less face prosecution); higher consumer spending; more government tax revenue (e.g. indirect taxes on spending).
- Negative implications: some employers hire fewer staff (e.g. 100 workers at 10.20 euro vs 200 at 5.10 euro); reduced hours; less competitive Irish exports (higher wages than some EU countries); knock-on increases for non-minimum wage workers wanting to keep their differential.
- A minimum wage is a price floor. Reasons: trade union demands, incentivise work, reduce poverty, reduce income inequality, raise living standards of the low-paid.
- Figure 9.11 (in words): labour demand and supply; a horizontal line Wmin above the equilibrium wage. No one supplies labour below Wmin; at Wmin supply exceeds demand, so there is excess supply of labour (unemployment); above Wmin the Law of Supply applies.
- Living wage: a wage that makes possible a minimum acceptable standard of living; 12.30 euro per hour sought in 2021 by trade unions and NGOs.
- Gig economy: independent workers (contractors, freelancers) working short-term or 'payment by task', e.g. Deliveroo riders.

WAGE DIFFERENTIALS
- 1. Nature of the job - risk (Gardai, prison officers); unsociable hours.
- 2. Skills/qualifications/training - a doctor (seven years) earns more than a nurse (four years); consultants more than junior doctors.
- 3. Responsibility - pilots, train drivers, brain surgeons.
- 4. Experience - incremental pay scales in the public sector.
- 5. Trade union membership - e.g. transport unions can cause major disruption, giving bargaining power.
- 6. Productivity - TV/radio personalities attracting big audiences (high MRP) negotiate high pay.
- 7. Innate talent - golfers, footballers, tennis players, musicians, comedians.

THE GENDER PAY GAP
- Gender pay gap: the difference between average gross earnings of female and male employees.
- 2018: men's average gross hourly earnings 14.8% higher in the EU; Ireland 14.4% (Eurostat).
- Unequal pay (different pay for men and women in the same job) is illegal; the gender pay gap compares averages across all employees.
- Causes: women over-represented in low-paid jobs and men in higher-paid jobs; the 'glass ceiling' (CEOs, ministers mostly men); women more likely to take career breaks, job share and maternity leave, missing promotion; high childcare costs (2019 average 184 euro per child per week; 251 euro in Dun Laoghaire-Rathdown) push a parent, usually the mother, out of work; more women in part-time work and in lower-paid professions (nursing, early childcare).
- Solutions: gender quotas (2019: 45 women-only professorships in Irish universities); family-friendly working (flexible hours, working from home); mandatory gender pay gap reporting (UK, over 250 employees; proposed in Ireland) - e.g. an airline with mostly male pilots and female flight attendants would be 'named and shamed', pushing it to recruit more female pilots (e.g. quotas) and more male flight attendants.

rows.explanation: Money for investment is borrowed, and the price paid is the interest rate.

The minimum payment needed to keep a factor in use
The return on a factor in excess of its supply price
The interest paid on borrowed capital
rows.explanation: Earnings above the supply price are economic rent.

options: The supply of land is fixed
rows.explanation: Gifts of nature are finite, so supply is perfectly inelastic.

Its earnings are residual - it is paid last

options: Negative - a higher rate lowers the MEC

If inflation is 10% and a worker's pay stays at 20,000 euro, then:

rows.explanation: The 7th worker would cost 40 euro but add only 20 euro in revenue.

options: The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns

Their output is too easy to measure
They produce no physical output and their service has no market price
rows.explanation: MPP is hard to measure for services, and public services are not sold in a market.

Unequal pay for the same job is illegal; the pay gap compares averages
Unequal pay compares average earnings of all workers

rows.prompt: Distinguish between a goods and services market and a factor market, and explain 'derived demand'.
rows.model_answer: In a goods and services market individuals buy goods and services to consume them, such as an ice cream or a haircut. In a factor market firms acquire factors of production, such as labour or oil, to produce goods and services. Demand for a factor is derived demand - it is wanted not for itself but for what it helps produce, e.g. timber to make tables.

rows.prompt: Outline four ways the government encourages entrepreneurship.
rows.model_answer: Grants and advice through Enterprise Ireland and the Local Enterprise Offices. Loans through Microfinance Ireland of up to 25,000 euro for small firms. Better infrastructure such as the National Broadband Plan. The Credit Review Office can force banks to lend to viable businesses, and investment in education gives a skilled workforce.

rows.prompt: Explain the marginal efficiency of capital and state three factors that affect it.
rows.model_answer: MEC is the extra profit from employing one extra unit of capital - the extra revenue it generates minus its cost, e.g. a 10,000 euro coffee machine making 14,000 euro gives an MEC of 4,000 euro. It is affected by the price of the output, the demand for the output, the cost of capital and the interest rate, and wear and tear.

rows.prompt: Define MPP and MRP and explain the Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns.
rows.model_answer: MPP is the extra output from employing one extra worker; MRP is the extra revenue from employing one extra worker (MPP x MR). The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns states that as more units of a variable factor such as labour are added to a fixed factor such as a pizza oven, the extra output eventually falls, e.g. because of bottlenecks.

rows.prompt: State four factors that determine the MRP of labour.
rows.model_answer: The skills, qualifications and experience of the workers. The quality of the capital they use, e.g. a high-spec oven. The ability of the manager to motivate staff and worker morale from conditions and pay. The selling price of the output.

rows.prompt: Distinguish between occupational and geographical mobility of labour, giving one influencing factor for each.
rows.model_answer: Occupational mobility is the willingness to move from one occupation to another; it is affected by the qualifications and training needed, e.g. a solicitor retraining as a doctor. Geographical mobility is the willingness to move location for work; it is affected by factors such as age, family situation and property prices.

rows.prompt: Name four reasons why wage rates differ between workers.
rows.model_answer: The nature of the job, such as risk or unsociable hours. Skills, qualifications and length of training. The degree of responsibility. Experience, trade union membership, productivity and innate talent also cause differences.

rows.prompt: Explain the gender pay gap and outline two measures the government could take to reduce it.
rows.model_answer: The gender pay gap is the difference between the average gross hourly earnings of male and female employees - 14.4% in Ireland in 2018. Measures include gender quotas for senior positions, family-friendly working conditions such as flexible hours, and mandatory gender pay gap reporting.

rows.prompt: A pizza restaurant sells pizzas at 10 euro each. Total output with 2, 3 and 4 workers is 25, 42 and 50 pizzas. (i) Calculate the MPP and MRP of the 3rd and 4th workers. (ii) How many workers would be hired at a wage of 80 euro? Explain. (iii) Explain two reasons why the MRP curve slopes downwards. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) 3rd worker: MPP = 42 - 25 = 17 pizzas; MRP = 17 x 10 = 170 euro. 4th worker: MPP = 50 - 42 = 8 pizzas; MRP = 8 x 10 = 80 euro. (ii) Four workers. Under MRP theory, the employer hires up to the point where the wage equals the MRP of the last worker hired; the 4th worker's MRP equals the 80 euro wage, so he is hired, and all workers are paid the MRP of the last worker. A 5th worker would add less revenue than his wage. (iii) 1. The Law of Diminishing Marginal Returns: as more workers are added to a fixed amount of capital, such as one pizza oven, bottlenecks occur - chefs get in each other's way - so each extra worker adds less output. 2. The Law of Demand: if the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, it must lower the price of all pizzas to sell the extra output, so the extra revenue from each worker falls, e.g. 50 pizzas at 10 euro = 500 euro but at 8 euro = 400 euro.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 8 marks: 4 figures x 2m. (ii) 7 marks: answer 3m + explanation 4m. (iii) 10 marks: 2 reasons x 5m (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation). Total 25 marks.

rows.prompt: (a) Explain, with the aid of a diagram, the effect on the labour market of a minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage. (b) Discuss the economic implications of increasing the minimum wage. (25 marks)
rows.model_answer: (a) Diagram (in words): wage rate on the vertical axis and quantity of labour on the horizontal; a downward-sloping demand for labour curve and an upward-sloping supply of labour curve meet at the equilibrium wage. A horizontal line Wmin is drawn above the equilibrium. At Wmin, quantity of labour supplied is greater than quantity demanded, so there is excess supply of labour, i.e. unemployment. No worker will supply labour below Wmin, and above Wmin the Law of Supply applies. The minimum wage acts as a price floor. (b) Positive: 1. A better standard of living for low-paid workers. 2. Exploitation is prevented, as employers paying less can be prosecuted. 3. Consumer spending rises as low-paid workers have more income, boosting demand. 4. Government tax revenue rises, e.g. from indirect taxes. Negative: 1. Some employers hire fewer staff to control costs. 2. Hours may be cut. 3. Irish exports become less competitive as labour costs are higher than in some EU countries. 4. Knock-on wage increases for experienced workers who want to keep their pay differential above the minimum.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 10 marks: diagram 6m (axes and curves 2m, equilibrium 1m, Wmin above equilibrium 1m, excess supply shown 2m) + explanation 4m. (b) 15 marks: 3 points x 5 marks (2 marks statement + 3 marks explanation); at least one positive and one negative.

rows.prompt: Outline the problems that labour shortages can cause for employers and the economy, and suggest three measures the government could take to address them. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Problems: 1. Employers may have to recruit lower-quality employees with poor qualifications or little experience, so productivity is lower. 2. Some vacancies cannot be filled, reducing quality of service, e.g. a busy restaurant short of waiting staff. 3. Employers must pay higher wages to attract and keep staff, causing wage drift and cost-push inflation. 4. Higher labour costs make Ireland less attractive for FDI. Measures: 1. More visas for non-EU workers, e.g. the Critical Skills Employment Permit for ICT professionals. 2. Encourage emigrants to return, e.g. the HSE 'Bring Them Home' campaign with a 1,500 euro relocation fee. 3. Incentivise training in shortage areas, e.g. STEM and the Springboard programme. 4. Reduce direct taxes, raise the minimum wage, reduce accommodation costs or provide childcare and other social infrastructure.
rows.marking_scheme: Problems: 2 points x 5m (2m statement + 3m explanation) = 10m. Measures: 2 points x 5m = 10m (credit any valid third measure within these). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: State and explain three factors that could cause the demand curve for labour to shift to the right, and two factors that could cause the supply curve for labour to shift to the right. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Demand shifts right: 1. A rise in demand for the firm's output - demand for labour is derived, so more demand for coffee means more baristas are needed. 2. State subsidies, e.g. JobsPlus gives employers up to 10,000 euro to hire people from the live register. 3. More FDI, attracted by low corporation tax, increases demand for workers in Ireland. (A fall in employers' PRSI would also lower the cost of employing workers.) Supply shifts right: 1. A rise in the working-age population, e.g. through immigration, returning emigrants or less emigration. 2. A rise in the labour force participation rate, so a larger share of those aged 16-66 are working or seeking work. (Greater occupational or geographical mobility of labour also increases supply.)
rows.marking_scheme: 5 factors x 4 marks (2 marks statement + 2 marks explanation). Total 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between unequal pay and the gender pay gap. Outline two causes of the gender pay gap and two measures to reduce it. (15 marks)
rows.model_answer: Unequal pay is paying men and women different rates for the same job, which is illegal. The gender pay gap is the difference between the average gross hourly earnings of all male and all female employees; it was 14.4% in Ireland in 2018. Causes: 1. Women are over-represented in lower-paid jobs and part-time work, while a 'glass ceiling' leaves senior roles dominated by men. 2. Career breaks, job sharing, maternity leave and high childcare costs (184 euro per child per week in 2019) interrupt women's career progression. Measures: 1. Mandatory gender pay gap reporting, as in the UK for firms with over 250 employees, would name and shame firms and push them to change. 2. Gender quotas for senior positions, e.g. 45 women-only professorships in 2019, or family-friendly working such as flexible hours.
rows.marking_scheme: Distinction 3 marks. Causes: 2 x 3m. Measures: 2 x 3m. Total 15 marks.
